title: A computational and experimental study of coflow laminar methane/air diffusion flames: Effects of fuel dilution, inlet velocity, and gravity
summary: SLICE nitrogen-diluted methane flames (CH4 0.4-1.0, mean fuel velocity 23-90 cm/s) in microgravity and 1 g, modelled with a vorticity-velocity code and sectional soot model: luminous length proportional to fuel-mixture mass flow, microgravity flames longer; shape set by methane flow, dilution secondary.

items.claim: Flame length proportional to fuel-mixture mass flow, longer in microgravity.
items.quote: Buoyant and nonbuoyant luminous flame lengths are proportional to the mass flow rate of the fuel mixture; computed and measured nonbuoyant flames are noticeably longer than their 1g counterparts

items.claim: Dilution negligible once shape is normalised by methane flow.
items.quote: the effect of fuel dilution on flame shape (i.e., flame length and flame radius) is negligible when the flame shape is normalized by the methane flow rate

notes: NTRS conference/preprint version (20150002322) of the Proc. Combust. Inst. 35 paper; the record already used it.

title: A Combined Experimental and Computational Study of Soot Formation in Normal and Microgravity Conditions
summary: Combined experiment/computation of sooting ethylene-air coflow flames in 1 g and on the ISS with two burner configurations (Yale and ACME). Simulations show 0-g flames longer, broader, cooler and sootier, an effect much smaller for the small ACME flame; the authors suspect the model mispredicts the thermal field and burner-lip heat transfer.

items.claim: Gravity effects on ethylene coflow flames are much weaker for the small ACME burner than for the Yale burner, in simulation; model likely mispredicts temperature (attribution of the ISS data to this investigation unconfirmed).
items.quote: However, in the case of the smaller ACME flame, these effects are significantly diminished.

notes: Taylor & Francis paywall; NTRS accepted manuscript (27530189361808) has no download. Abstract via OpenAlex. The abstract does not say which ISS experiment supplied the microgravity data; the "Yale" burner may be the SLICE hardware but this is not confirmed, so nothing was added to the record. Listed under both PSI-106 and PSI-107; read once.

title: Effects of Fuel Dilution and Gravity on Laminar Coflow Methane-Air Diffusion Flames: A Computational and Experimental Investigation
summary: Conference version (Cao, Bennett, Ma, Giassi, Stocker, Takahashi, Long, Smooke) of the SLICE fuel-dilution study [0]; same authors and topic.
notes: No DOI; not on NTRS under this title, nor on Semantic Scholar/OpenAlex with text. Its content is assumed to match [0], which was read.

title: An experimental and computational study of soot formation in a coflow jet flame under microgravity and normal gravity
summary: SLICE 100% methane flame (3.23 mm nozzle, 46 cm/s fuel, 18 cm/s coflow) in microgravity vs 1 g: microgravity flame taller, wider, cooler (~200 K) and sootier; soot moves from centreline to wings; model captures shape and soot location but underestimates soot, especially in microgravity.

items.claim: Soot shifts from centreline (1 g) to wings (microgravity); model captures shape, underpredicts soot.
items.quote: The distribution of peak soot was also found to shift from the centerline of the flame at 1 g to the wings at μ g.

items.claim: The record says peak soot volume fraction was "about 8 times higher" in microgravity. The paper's conclusion, allowing for uncertainty in the soot dispersion exponent and temperature, bounds the increase at about 4 to 8 times; ~8 is the upper value.
items.quote: the microgravity flames were found to be sootier than normal gravity flames by a factor of approximately 4 to 8 in terms of the peak soot volume fraction

notes: NTRS preprint (20140017780) of the Proc. Combust. Inst. 35 paper; the record already used its results section.

title: Analysis of CH* concentration and flame heat release rate in laminar coflow diffusion flames under microgravity and normal gravity
summary: Journal paper (Giassi et al., Combust. Flame 2016) on CH* chemiluminescence and heat release in SLICE coflow flames.
notes: No abstract found (Crossref, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar; NTRS has no copy under this title); Elsevier paywall. The record already uses the same authors' NTRS presentations 20160012298 and 20160010264 on the same results (findings[6]).
